questions.title: Instrument the actual bottleneck
questions.stem: An animation studio blames translation for subtitle delays. Editors translate quickly but wait days for terminology approval. Stage timings are unmeasured, and licensor approval cannot change this quarter. What should establish whether AI can meet the delivery goal?

options.text: Benchmark translation accuracy and proceed if Claude exceeds the existing editorial quality threshold.
options.why: Translation quality matters later, but a quality benchmark cannot establish that faster translation addresses the dominant delivery delay.

options.text: Prototype automatic terminology approval before revisiting the licensor agreement with the business sponsor.
options.why: This changes an explicitly fixed authority boundary, so the prototype cannot validate the proposed intervention under current constraints.

options.text: Measure time by workflow state and compare addressable translation time with the delivery target.
options.why: State-level evidence distinguishes work the proposed system can accelerate from waiting time outside its authority and scope.

options.text: Estimate subtitle token costs and prioritize the smallest affordable model for the translation workflow.
options.why: Inference economics optimize a candidate solution without establishing that its addressable interval can materially improve the stated outcome.

questions.decision: Frame the problem around delivery states before choosing a model. If approval waiting dominates and cannot change, even perfect translation acceleration may miss the target. Establish the baseline, addressable time and authority constraints, then decide whether to proceed or redefine scope.

questions.title: Separate prediction from explanation
questions.stem: A heating operator has a validated hourly demand predictor. Dispatchers need explanations using weather notes and maintenance reports. The owner requires numeric forecasts to remain under existing validation. Select TWO recommendations that address the explanation need.

options.text: Treat explanations as provisional forecasts and let dispatchers choose the most credible weather-adjusted value.
options.why: This conflates a communication aid with an alternative prediction channel and transfers an unresolved validation problem to dispatchers.

options.text: Let Claude correct forecast values when maintenance notes are newer than the predictor’s inputs.
options.why: Recency alone supplies neither validated correction logic nor delegated authority to change the numeric output in this design.

options.text: Test explanation faithfulness and dispatcher comprehension separately from the existing numeric forecast acceptance tests.
options.why: The new capability has its own failure modes; preserving forecast tests alone does not establish useful, supported explanations.

options.text: Keep the predictor authoritative and have Claude explain supplied drivers using linked operational evidence.
options.why: This places language generation around the existing predictor while preserving the owner’s explicitly assigned authority over numeric forecasts.

options.text: Replace the predictor with Claude and validate agreement on average totals over one historical month.
options.why: Monthly average agreement can conceal hourly errors and does not satisfy the owner’s requirement to preserve the validated predictor.

questions.decision: The architecture should separate numeric prediction from evidence-based explanation. Preserve the validated service as the authoritative forecast and evaluate the language layer against its actual job: explaining supplied drivers clearly without inventing causes or changing values. This directly addresses the unmet user need.

questions.title: Bind approval to application state
questions.stem: A museum curator approves a collection transfer, but a background process can later change its destination. The asynchronous execution worker checks only approval for the transfer ID. How should it ensure approval covers the destination actually used?

options.text: Keep transfer-ID approval and notify the curator when background updates change the destination before execution.
options.why: Notification supplies awareness but does not stop execution under an approval that no longer covers the current destination.

options.text: Ask Claude immediately before execution whether the original approval still applies to the transfer summary.
options.why: A semantic similarity judgment cannot enforce that the actual destination and version equal those approved by the curator.

options.text: Bind approval to version and destination; reject execution if either differs from the approved state.
options.why: Version-bound authorization prevents an approval for one destination being reused after the application state changes before execution.

options.text: Lock destination editing in the curator interface while permitting background updates to the worker’s destination.
options.why: An interface restriction leaves the identified background mutation path available and therefore fails the stated exact-state requirement.

questions.decision: Approval is an input to execution, not a permanent property of a transfer ID. Check a version or digest that includes the destination at commit time. If relevant state changes, return the case for renewed approval before any instruction is executed.

questions.title: Carry authorized memory forward
questions.stem: A seasonal grant assistant must retain approved project facts between sessions. Users can lose project access, and facts can change. Engineers propose loading a summary by user ID at login. Select TWO necessary additions.

options.text: Keep generated summaries accessible after project access revocation because they belong to the requesting user.
options.why: Generation does not erase the underlying project restriction; previously authorized access does not establish indefinite permission to reuse facts.

options.text: Store summaries under project display names and let Claude infer which project the user means.
options.why: Display names can collide or change, and model inference does not replace explicit identity and permission binding during assembly.

options.text: Allow owner corrections and rebuild affected summaries when approved source narratives change or are withdrawn.
options.why: Durable memory can become stale, and a correction mechanism prevents obsolete narrative facts persisting beyond the approved source.

options.text: Store project identity, provenance and revision with facts; recheck project access before loading them.
options.why: Memory selection must reflect current authorization; linking facts to their source project enables access checks and later correction.

options.text: Retain all summaries and load the longest version to preserve the most original approved details.
options.why: Length does not establish authority, freshness or correctness; retaining obsolete summaries without revision selection compounds the stale-state problem.

questions.decision: Memory belongs in a governed context-assembly path. Persist compact facts with stable project identity and provenance, verify access at retrieval time, and let owners correct or withdraw them. The useful continuity comes from authorized current state, not automatic loading of historical user summaries.

questions.title: Bound iterative refinement
questions.stem: A script critic detects missing spatial cues. One revision improves blind reviewers’ comprehension; further revisions can oscillate between concision and detail. Release needs bounded processing time, and editors accept unresolved cases. Which pattern fits?

options.text: Restart generation whenever the critic finds a failure, letting completion time vary with script complexity.
options.why: Unbounded restarts preserve the oscillation and conflict with the stated requirement for a stable maximum processing time.

options.text: Generate a fixed set of independent scripts and select the shortest without assessing spatial cues.
options.why: Shortest length is not the validated accessibility criterion, so voting among drafts discards the evidence motivating the change.

options.text: Route by word count to concise or detailed prompts, retiring the critic after both prompts deploy.
options.why: Word count does not establish spatial-cue completeness, and removing the measured critique step has no supporting evaluation evidence.

options.text: Bound draft-and-critique cycles with clear pass rules; send scripts still failing to the editorial queue.
options.why: A bounded loop captures the demonstrated revision benefit while giving the system a definite stopping point and unresolved-case path.

questions.decision: An evaluator–optimizer pattern fits because critique measurably improves the output. The time constraint changes its termination design: cap iterations, evaluate explicit criteria, and expose unresolved cases for manual handling. A useful critic does not justify an unbounded attempt to satisfy competing objectives.

questions.title: Parallel checks need a join rule
questions.stem: A food-labeling platform checks allergens, translation and dimensions on one frozen artwork revision. The checks are independent and all mandatory, but the prototype releases after two pass. Which design meets the requirement without unnecessary sequencing?

options.text: Let an orchestrator choose checks, requesting the remainder only when its initial assessment is uncertain.
options.why: The checks are already specified as mandatory, so making their execution discretionary conflicts with the agreed quality policy.

options.text: Keep two-of-three release and give the strongest model the check that fails most often.
options.why: Improving one checker does not satisfy the owner’s requirement that all three mandatory checks pass before release occurs.

options.text: Run checks concurrently and release only when all required results pass for the frozen revision.
options.why: Parallel execution is compatible with mandatory checks when the join condition requires every result and binds them to one revision.

options.text: Run checks sequentially, release after the second pass and retain the third result for audit.
options.why: Sequential order adds latency while the early release condition still omits a mandatory check from the actual release decision.

questions.decision: Use parallel sectioning for independent checks, coupled with a deterministic all-required join. Bind every result to the frozen artwork revision so late results cannot authorize changed artwork. The architectural issue is the completion condition, rather than whether concurrency itself is appropriate.

questions.title: Make specialist results mergeable
questions.stem: Three specialists research a storm’s weather, vessel tracks and port closures in parallel. Their reports disagree on event times and confirmation status, blocking synthesis. Parallel work meets the deadline. Select TWO changes that improve reconstruction reliability.

options.text: Make the report with most observations authoritative and align the other reports to its timeline.
options.why: Observation count does not establish source reliability, and forced harmonization can conceal unresolved evidence rather than verify the reconstruction.

options.text: Run specialists sequentially with identical prompts so later workers can repeat earlier workers’ conclusions.
options.why: Serial repetition sacrifices independence and latency without supplying the missing event schema or resolving the source evidence conflicts.

options.text: Require UTC timestamps, source references and observed-versus-inferred status in a shared event schema.
options.why: A common representation makes findings comparable while preserving uncertainty and evidence needed to judge conflicts during final synthesis.

options.text: Have the lead check material conflicts against evidence and record disagreements that remain unresolved.
options.why: Verification and explicit conflict handling prevent plausible but incompatible specialist assertions becoming an unsupported single account of events.

options.text: Give each specialist the lead’s full conversation and preserve free-form reports with local narrative styles.
options.why: Extra context does not solve incompatible evidence contracts, and free-form reports preserve the specific merge failure described here.

questions.decision: Keep independent research parallel, but standardize the handoff contract. The lead needs comparable times, provenance and uncertainty to reconcile findings. Material conflicts require evidence checks or an explicit unresolved result; producing a smooth narrative is not sufficient when the sources disagree.

questions.title: Account for coordination overhead
questions.stem: Three parallel corridor studies need different evidence bundles but share rolling-stock assumptions. A lead must reconcile them within a strict total token budget. Select THREE measures needed to assess quality and economics before approving this multi-agent design.

options.text: Estimate cost from the longest worker output because parallel workers do not add overall usage.
options.why: Parallelism reduces some elapsed time but does not make other workers’ tokens disappear from the system’s aggregate resource consumption.

options.text: Average individual corridor report scores to estimate the quality of the final cross-corridor recommendation.
options.why: Component scores cannot establish that the synthesis reconciles shared resources; a good local report may imply an infeasible combined plan.

options.text: Budget all worker context, duplicated evidence and lead synthesis tokens per completed study.
options.why: Total system consumption includes coordination and repeated context; counting only the final answer would understate the architecture’s real cost.

options.text: Maintain shared assumptions and require the lead to reconcile rolling-stock conflicts before final recommendations.
options.why: Independent studies still share consequential assumptions, so an explicit reconciliation step is needed before their recommendations can be combined.

options.text: Compare against a single-agent baseline with identical corridor coverage and a final-recommendation quality rubric.
options.why: Comparable coverage and outcome criteria reveal whether the extra orchestration improves the actual planning task enough to justify its cost.

questions.decision: Parallel corridors are a plausible decomposition, but the decision depends on measured end-to-end value. Compare against a fair baseline, account for every participant’s consumption, and reconcile shared assumptions explicitly. Independence in evidence collection does not imply that the final planning decisions are independent.

questions.title: Preserve cross-document dependencies
questions.stem: Aerospace reviewers need to decompose a certification package that overwhelms one prompt. Local checks find every required test, but miss a controller referencing a sensor test from an older interface. Which design also detects cross-package incompatibility?

options.text: Extract versioned requirements and interfaces, check links across packages, then synthesize release advice.
options.why: Structured local findings preserve detail while an explicit dependency pass tests relationships that cannot be judged within one isolated package.

options.text: Assign one reviewer per document and send only failed local tests to the release board.
options.why: A passing local test may reference an incompatible interface revision; excluding it prevents the cross-package comparison the defect requires.

options.text: Increase overlap between adjacent chunks and let the summarizer infer version conflicts from reviewer prose.
options.why: Chunk overlap may help local continuity but does not guarantee that distant interface dependencies are represented or systematically checked.

options.text: Average subsystem reviewers’ overall pass scores to produce a single recommendation on package readiness.
options.why: Averages discard the revision references needed to detect compatibility defects and can hide a blocking dependency behind strong local scores.

questions.decision: Decompose by subsystem, but define the synthesis inputs around requirements, versions and dependencies rather than verdicts alone. Cross-package compatibility is its own obligation. A final dependency check can detect a locally valid test attached to the wrong interface without recreating the entire original context.

questions.title: Compute value on completed work
questions.stem: Two parcel-description workflows use the same historical workload. Both pass legal accuracy review; accepted descriptions have equal value. The table includes all operating and review costs, equally excluding build costs. Select TWO conclusions about expense per accepted description.

options.text: Choose A: lower total operating expense establishes lower unit cost regardless of the accepted volume.
options.why: Lower absolute expense does not establish lower expense per accepted description when the alternatives produce different numbers of accepted outputs.

options.text: Report equal cost performance because both passed the quality gate and both exclude build costs.
options.why: Meeting the same quality threshold makes comparison feasible but does not erase the observed difference in expense per accepted result.

options.text: Choose B for operating unit cost, assessing excluded build costs separately before broader investment approval.
options.why: B meets the quality gate and wins the stated denominator; omitted investment costs remain relevant to a separate full business case.

options.text: B costs 15 currency units per accepted description; A costs 18 on this workload.
options.why: Dividing total included expense by accepted outputs gives comparable completed-work economics: 7,200/400 is 18 and 9,000/600 is 15.

options.text: Treat B’s 200 extra accepted descriptions as guaranteed payroll savings after passing the accuracy gate.
options.why: Additional output establishes capacity, not an automatic reduction in staffing expense; cash savings depend on an explicit realizable operating change.

questions.decision: Use the business denominator specified in the decision: accepted descriptions. A costs 7,200/400 = 18 units and B costs 9,000/600 = 15. B wins this operating comparison. A full investment approval still needs build costs and a defensible account of realizable benefits.

questions.title: Deadline slack is not a guarantee
questions.stem: A film archive needs overnight summaries between midnight and a 06:00 handoff. Missing summaries require costly editor intervention. The team proposes Message Batches because many finish quickly. What should determine whether batching fits this deadline?

options.text: Measure batch completion distributions and plan a deadline fallback; typical speed cannot guarantee six-hour completion.
options.why: Batches can take longer or expire, so a six-hour operational deadline requires workload evidence and a defined treatment of unfinished items.

options.text: Approve batching because the documented 24-hour processing window guarantees completion before the next scheduled handoff.
options.why: A 24-hour window exceeds the stated six-hour deadline, and expiry behavior means even that window is not a universal success guarantee.

options.text: Keep every request synchronous because asynchronous processing cannot inform deadline-sensitive operational decisions usefully.
options.why: Asynchrony does not preclude useful measured performance; an evidence-backed fallback may make partial batching economically viable for this workload.

options.text: Choose batching if the published token discount exceeds the editor’s hourly wage in currency units.
options.why: Token discounts and hourly wages use incompatible denominators; the analysis must include unfinished-item probability and the actual intervention cost.

questions.decision: A pricing advantage supports a candidate architecture, not a deadline guarantee. Measure the archive’s workload, track unfinished items against the handoff cutoff and define a tested fallback. The business case must include fallback cost and failure risk as well as nominal batch discounts.

questions.title: Route on measured detectable need
questions.stem: A patent-search product’s fast configuration handles bibliographic lookups well. A stronger one improves ambiguous novelty comparisons. Intent is detectable before retrieval; generated confidence is poorly calibrated. Both use a common evaluation set. Which routing strategy fits?

options.text: Call the fast configuration first and escalate only when its generated confidence falls below a threshold.
options.why: The proposed gate depends on confidence that is explicitly poorly calibrated, so it cannot reliably identify the segment needing stronger reasoning.

options.text: Route detected novelty comparisons to the stronger configuration and bibliographic lookups to the validated fast one.
options.why: The detectable task distinction corresponds to measured capability needs; monitoring classification mistakes checks whether routing preserves the observed benefit.

options.text: Randomly split all queries and favor the configuration with the lowest average weekly token count.
options.why: Random allocation can support experimentation but does not exploit the validated task distinction or establish quality on each routed segment.

options.text: Use the stronger configuration universally because its novelty-comparison gains show the fast one is unsuitable.
options.why: Evidence on one difficult segment does not invalidate the faster configuration’s successful bibliographic performance or justify its unnecessary replacement everywhere.

questions.decision: Route using a distinction that is observable before the model answers and linked to measured task performance. Validate the complete router-plus-model system, including misroutes. A stronger model’s benefit on one segment does not establish its value on already satisfactory simple lookups.

questions.title: Test the complete configuration
questions.stem: A geological survey compares a stronger model at modest reasoning effort against a smaller model with retries. A shared glossary is cached, but reuse across models is uncertain. Select TWO measurements for acceptable quality at lowest cost per completed classification.

options.text: Measure accepted quality and total cost, including attempts, escalations, repeated context and validation failures.
options.why: The complete execution path determines delivered quality and economics; comparing first calls alone would omit the candidate cascade’s principal overhead.

options.text: Count only accepted outputs and omit failed retries because they add nothing to delivered records.
options.why: Failed attempts still consume resources and time, making their exclusion an inaccurate estimate of cost per completed classification task.

options.text: Measure cache-read and cache-write usage on each model path rather than assuming cross-model glossary reuse.
options.why: Cache behavior affects the cascade’s consumption, and model-scoped matching means escalation cannot automatically inherit the initial model’s cached prefix.

options.text: Let each model’s owner choose a different mineral set suited to that model’s processing strengths.
options.why: Different favorable workloads prevent a fair comparison and can hide capability failures on the shared task distribution the survey must serve.

options.text: Compare advertised token prices and treat repeated glossary tokens as free once either model caches them.
options.why: Advertised unit price omits retries, and caching by one model does not establish free cross-model reuse for subsequent escalation requests.

questions.decision: Compare deployed configurations rather than model labels or list prices. The smaller-model cascade must pay for initial calls, validations, retries and actual cache behavior. Use the same representative workload and success rubric, then choose among configurations that meet the quality constraint on completed work.

questions.title: Give conflicting instructions an owner
questions.stem: An auction assistant’s shared policy requires estimate ranges, while a local prompt requests one spreadsheet value. The policy owner rejects point estimates; the spreadsheet can accept two columns. Which prompt and interface change resolves the conflicting outputs?

options.text: Keep both instructions and add more range examples so most replies follow the shared policy.
options.why: Examples may bias behavior but leave incompatible instructions unresolved, so the remaining output contract still demands a prohibited single estimate.

options.text: Place the point-estimate instruction last so the spreadsheet requirement consistently takes precedence over policy.
options.why: Recency cannot grant a local integration permission to override the explicitly authoritative policy owner’s requirement for estimated ranges.

options.text: Let Claude choose the appropriate rule per item and explain its choice in free text.
options.why: Delegating the policy conflict to generation produces case-dependent behavior when the owners have already supplied a compatible and authoritative resolution.

options.text: Make range policy authoritative and version the output contract with spreadsheet-ready lower and upper bounds.
options.why: The permitted interface change removes the contradictory demand while preserving both the policy owner’s decision and the downstream need for structured values.

questions.decision: Resolve the contradiction in requirements and the output contract before tuning language. The range policy remains authoritative, while two numeric fields satisfy the import need. Version and test that combined change so later reviewers can see which rule governs the interface and why.

questions.title: Teach the boundary that fails
questions.stem: An oral-history archive has stable output formatting but mislabels passages combining firsthand events with quoted accounts. Curators have adjudicated these boundary cases and can explain the rule. Which prompting experiment should precede a model change?

options.text: Add varied adjudicated boundary examples, then test new boundary and ordinary passages for regressions.
options.why: The failure concerns an ambiguous decision boundary, so examples should teach that distinction and be tested beyond the examples themselves.

options.text: Request longer label explanations and choose the label whose explanation reproduces the most source words.
options.why: Explanation length and lexical overlap do not establish correct application of the category rule to mixed-perspective passages in this dataset.

options.text: Add more historical documents to every request so Claude can infer which witnesses are generally credible.
options.why: Credibility is a different task from the stipulated passage-labeling rule, and extra documents do not teach the adjudicated category boundary.

options.text: Add easily classified eyewitness examples with matching formatting to improve consistent reproduction of the schema.
options.why: Formatting is already stable, and easy examples do not demonstrate the quoted-account distinction responsible for the observed classification errors.

questions.decision: Use examples for the judgment boundary that evidence shows is failing. Include contrasting adjudicated cases, then hold out unseen variants and retain ordinary-case coverage. The experiment should establish whether examples improve application of the curator’s rule, rather than merely making answers longer or more uniform.

questions.title: Recover durable facts after compaction
questions.stem: After summarizing investigations, a maintenance assistant confuses an approved machine isolation state with an earlier tentative state. The authoritative control system remains safely queryable. Select TWO changes that preserve continuity without treating summaries as current-state proof.

options.text: Carry forward the longest assistant message because its detailed narrative necessarily preserves the authoritative state.
options.why: Length does not establish confirmation or recency, and the longest message may preserve a tentative state rather than the approved one.

options.text: Keep confirmed IDs, source timestamps and unresolved hypotheses in a compact record separating observations from proposals.
options.why: A structured record protects essential investigation facts while making their age and evidentiary status explicit after conversational details are summarized.

options.text: Require operators to repeat all observations and remove the control-system integration after each context compaction.
options.why: This discards a safe authoritative source and burdens the operator without establishing a reliable method for distinguishing historical from current state.

options.text: Increase the summary output cap and treat every mentioned state as current until the next session.
options.why: A larger summary can still collapse temporal distinctions, and an output limit cannot establish the freshness of an external machine state.

options.text: Refresh consequential machine state through the authorized control-system read endpoint before current operational recommendations.
options.why: Current state must come from its authoritative source; preserving a summary does not establish that an earlier observation still holds.

questions.decision: Preserve compact investigation state, but maintain its provenance and uncertainty. Operational state can change independently of the conversation, so refresh it from the authoritative system before consequential use. Compaction should reduce conversational bulk while retaining links to truth, not turn historical text into a live control record.

questions.title: Trim outputs without losing invariants
questions.stem: A library renewal task needs loan IDs, due dates, eligibility and account restrictions from a large patron record. Restrictions can block otherwise eligible renewals. Which context change reduces payload while preserving a correct recommendation for the signed-in patron?

options.text: Summarize the record in prose and omit restriction fields when space runs short for typical patrons.
options.why: Dropping a rare but decisive restriction changes the decision semantics and can authorize recommendations that fail the circulation system’s explicit rules.

options.text: Cache the full patron record indefinitely by display name to eliminate input context costs on later requests.
options.why: Caching does not remove context content or guarantee indefinite freshness, and display names do not provide a safe stable identity binding.

options.text: Return a typed renewal projection with required loan fields, restriction flags and source revision metadata.
options.why: Task-specific projection removes unrelated patron data while retaining the conditions and state references needed to judge and safely execute a renewal.

options.text: Return only due dates and infer renewal eligibility from whether each item has passed its scheduled date.
options.why: Due dates do not encode renewal eligibility or account restrictions, so inference from them cannot preserve the required circulation rules.

questions.decision: Optimize context around the task’s sufficient information, not the smallest possible payload. A renewal projection can omit unrelated patron details while retaining eligibility, restrictions, identity and version. Those fields preserve the domain invariants that the later action must validate against the current circulation state.

questions.title: Diagnose prefix identity before TTL
questions.stem: An architecture studio’s cached manual gets requests every minute, but cache reads stay zero. A random request ID starts the prefix; minimum cache length is met. Select TWO changes that address and verify this miss mechanism.

options.text: Shorten the manual below minimum cache length so reuse becomes automatic without explicit cache boundaries.
options.why: Falling below the minimum prevents caching, and the scenario already establishes that length eligibility is satisfied before the proposed change.

options.text: Extend cache lifetime but keep the random leading identifier so entries have more time to become visible.
options.why: Entries that never match cannot be read regardless of lifetime, and the minute-long interval does not explain this specific prefix-identity failure.

options.text: Compare creation and read tokens before and after using the same model and stable manual revision.
options.why: Usage fields establish whether the reordered stable prefix is actually reused under controlled conditions rather than merely marked as cacheable.

options.text: Add cache boundaries throughout the manual while keeping the random identifier ahead of every boundary.
options.why: A changing element before every candidate boundary still prevents matching the corresponding prefixes, so additional boundaries do not repair the mechanism.

options.text: Place stable manual content before the cache boundary and the changing request identifier after it.
options.why: Cache matching depends on prefix identity, so moving the changing identifier removes the stated cause of nonmatching cached content across requests.

questions.decision: Fix the changing prefix before experimenting with TTL. Stable instructions and manual content must precede per-request identifiers for reusable matching. Verify the result through actual read and creation usage on the same model and manual revision; a configured cache boundary alone is not evidence of a hit.

video_evidence.concept: Cache reuse depends on prefix and lifetime

questions.title: Load procedures by task
questions.stem: A botanical institute’s long accession procedure is irrelevant to most field-trip requests. Accession work must use the full validated sequence. Which design reduces irrelevant context and supports reviewed updates across the institute’s assistant environments?

options.text: Install the procedure in one assistant surface and assume synchronization distributes its skill to API and coding environments.
options.why: Shared format does not establish automatic cross-environment deployment; the architecture needs an explicit distribution and version-verification mechanism for supported clients.

options.text: Use a short accession reminder and let Claude reconstruct procedural details from its general botanical knowledge.
options.why: The owner requires the full validated sequence, and general reconstruction cannot establish that omitted procedural steps remain correct and complete.

options.text: Package a versioned accession skill, load it for relevant tasks and deploy reviewed versions to each environment.
options.why: Task-specific loading avoids unrelated procedural context, while versioned explicit deployment preserves the validated sequence and makes environment coverage reviewable.

options.text: Include the procedure in every request and cache its prefix to reduce field-trip conversation token prices.
options.why: Caching may change cost but leaves irrelevant instructions in every conversation, which does not address the stated context-selection problem.

questions.decision: Move rarely used procedures behind task-specific loading without abridging the required sequence. Treat the package as a versioned artifact and verify deployment in every intended environment. Context reduction comes from selecting the correct procedure for the task, while release control preserves the approved operational content.

video_evidence.concept: Load a procedure for relevant tasks

questions.title: Scope tools by business operation
questions.stem: A sports assistant explains published fixtures through a generic query tool whose credential also reads unpublished disciplinary records. A read-only replica still exposes every table. Which change directly limits capability while preserving fixture explanations?

options.text: Offer published-fixture lookup by competition and status; enforce access to returned records in server code.
options.why: The narrow business operation removes unrelated data access and makes publication and competition constraints enforceable at the server boundary.

options.text: Keep generic queries with required justifications and review questionable access after federation staff report problems.
options.why: A justification and retrospective review can aid auditing but do not remove the assistant’s unnecessary authority to retrieve disciplinary information.

options.text: Return all table names with shorter descriptions to reduce context use and distraction during fixture queries.
options.why: Short descriptions reduce information rather than authority; the same credential still permits querying the unpublished records identified in the scenario.

options.text: Use the generic tool on a read-only replica and describe disciplinary-record exclusions in its instructions.
options.why: Read-only access still exposes unrelated confidential records, and descriptive exclusions do not enforce the required record-level restriction in the server.

questions.decision: Reduce capability at the interface and credential boundaries together. A published-fixture operation can enforce exactly which records the assistant needs. Moving the same broad read authority to a replica protects writes but does not address the unrelated confidential information available to the model.

questions.title: Validate the intended recipient
questions.stem: An MCP HTTP gateway accepts an authentic, unexpired token intended for a microscopy portal, then forwards it unchanged to a specimen API. Under the cited authorization specification, select TWO corrections at these token boundaries.

options.text: Accept only tokens issued for the MCP gateway and reject the microscopy-portal token there.
options.why: Authenticity and expiry do not establish intended audience; the gateway must validate that the access token was issued for its own resource.

options.text: Forward tokens over TLS and treat transport encryption as sufficient protection against incorrect upstream audiences.
options.why: TLS protects transport confidentiality and integrity but does not change a token’s intended recipient or supply missing resource authorization.

options.text: Use a separately authorized specimen-API credential instead of forwarding the gateway’s inbound access token unchanged.
options.why: The upstream API requires its own authorization context; MCP token passthrough is forbidden and does not establish appropriate downstream delegation.

options.text: Accept the portal token because the consortium’s shared issuer grants equivalent authorization across its applications.
options.why: A trusted issuer can issue tokens for different audiences, so shared issuance does not grant interchangeability between the portal and gateway.

options.text: Shorten token lifetimes while accepting all consortium audiences to remove the gateway’s confused-deputy risk.
options.why: Short duration limits exposure time but leaves the gateway accepting credentials intended for another application and forwarding them across boundaries.

questions.decision: Validate each token at the boundary for which it was issued. The MCP gateway must reject an authentic portal-only token; upstream access uses a separately authorized credential rather than passthrough. Issuer trust, TLS and short lifetime are useful controls but do not replace audience binding.

questions.title: Recheck authority at execution
questions.stem: Event organizers can lose access while attendee exports wait in a queue. Jobs retain requester and event IDs, but workers use broad credentials and trust submission-time checks. Which change prevents delivery after requester access is revoked?

options.text: Include the organizer’s role in the prompt and ask Claude to decline normally unauthorized exports.
options.why: A role description is not a current event-level authorization check, and the model cannot infer a revocation from historical queue data.

options.text: Export immediately with broad credentials and retain the artifact indefinitely pending a future fresh approval.
options.why: Early export does not solve unauthorized later delivery and creates an unnecessary retained artifact without the requested current authorization control.

options.text: Recheck requester-to-event access before reading data and before delivery through an access-controlled artifact link.
options.why: Queued work crosses time boundaries, so current authorization must govern both data access and delivery rather than a stale submission-time decision.

options.text: Encrypt queued payloads and retain submission-time authorization because encryption makes subsequent permission changes irrelevant.
options.why: Encryption protects stored payloads but does not renew the requester’s authority or prevent delivery after their event access is revoked.

questions.decision: A submission-time check authorizes submission, not unlimited future access. Queue workers must carry stable requester and event identity and validate current authority at consequential boundaries. Access-controlled delivery also prevents an export created legitimately from becoming available through a stale public or bearer link after revocation.

questions.title: Measure the end-to-end tail
questions.stem: A disaster-mapping service needs incident cards within P95 2.4 seconds without weakening evidence accuracy. Component durations correlate during large incidents, which current traces exclude. Select THREE actions for a defensible accuracy–latency release decision.

options.text: Compare candidate evidence accuracy against the unchanged gate on the same representative cases and rubric.
options.why: A latency gain is only feasible if the candidate still satisfies the independent accuracy constraint under a comparable evaluation workload.

options.text: Use linked spans to find critical-path changes and verify resulting service P95 under representative load.
options.why: Traces explain likely bottlenecks, while complete workload measurement establishes whether the proposed optimization improves the required user-visible tail.

options.text: Exclude large incidents from release testing to maintain comparability with the earlier demonstration workload.
options.why: Those bursts are within the service obligation, so excluding them preserves a biased benchmark that cannot establish the stated latency requirement.

options.text: Choose the smallest sum of component P95s because correlation makes it the exact service P95.
options.why: Correlation does not make marginal percentiles additive; summation can neither establish the exact tail nor replace representative end-to-end measurement.

options.text: Measure end-to-end latency including large incidents rather than equating summed component percentiles with service percentiles.
options.why: Percentiles do not add generally, and the missing correlated-load periods are material to the service tail under the stated requirement.

questions.decision: The decision needs joint feasibility: evidence accuracy plus the actual end-to-end tail under representative traffic. Component spans help locate the critical path, but summing their P95 values does not establish service P95. Include the omitted burst regime and measure the complete candidate before release.

questions.title: Trace the effective configuration
questions.stem: A university assistant cites wrong policy revisions despite normal API success and latency. Feature flags choose retrieval aliases; prompts deploy independently. Which observation design reconstructs one bad answer’s evidence path without unrestricted logging of raw student content?

options.text: Log the application commit and infer prompt and index versions from those current during investigation.
options.why: Independently deployed prompts and aliases can change after the request, so current values cannot reconstruct the historical effective configuration reliably.

options.text: Log request, index revision, resolved flags, prompt, model and source IDs in access-controlled trace records.
options.why: The effective configuration crosses independently deployed components, so correlated resolved identifiers connect an answer to its actual retrieval and generation path.

options.text: Store raw requests in general analytics and match similar wording to estimate the index used.
options.why: Similar content does not establish the resolved configuration, and unrestricted raw storage adds exposure without supplying the missing version correlation.

options.text: Alert on unsuccessful HTTP responses and use their frequency to detect incorrect policy citations.
options.why: Incorrect citations may accompany successful API responses, so transport-status alerts do not reconstruct the evidence revision behind the reported content failure.

questions.decision: Trace resolved runtime choices rather than only deployed code. The answer depends on the index alias target, feature flag, prompt and model used for that request. Structured correlation with source identifiers supports diagnosis while access controls and minimization avoid creating an unnecessary raw-content repository.

questions.title: Version contextual metadata with evidence
questions.stem: A bulletin contextualizer sometimes labels old engineering clauses with the latest revision’s date before embedding. Search then presents obsolete clauses as current. Select TWO changes addressing provenance and revision selection.

options.text: Retrieve more chunks and prefer the contextualized text with the most words matching the query.
options.why: Additional incorrectly labeled chunks and lexical overlap do not establish which revision is authoritative for the requested equipment and effective date.

options.text: Use authoritative equipment and revision metadata, keeping original source spans separate from generated context.
options.why: Authoritative metadata prevents generated context from silently redefining the source revision, while separate spans preserve what the original evidence actually states.

options.text: Rewrite contextual descriptions more fluently and discard original metadata to simplify the generator’s reading task.
options.why: Fluency does not establish factual provenance, and discarding authoritative metadata removes the reliable version facts needed to repair this failure.

options.text: Test revision-aware retrieval on current and superseded bulletins, including queries resembling superseded wording.
options.why: These cases test the exact temporal selection failure and ensure semantic similarity cannot override the intended effective-version constraints unnoticed.

options.text: Index only each section’s latest-ingested file, treating ingestion time as official effective-date and revision order.
options.why: Ingestion time may reflect delayed imports or reprocessing, so it cannot substitute for authoritative effective dates and document revision relationships.

questions.decision: Contextual text can improve retrieval, but it remains derived material. Preserve source text and authoritative version metadata, constrain retrieval to the relevant effective edition, and test superseded near-matches. The repair must address provenance and temporal selection rather than merely retrieve more plausible passages.

questions.title: Migrate indexes as complete versions
questions.stem: A fashion archive replaces its multilingual embedding model. Equal vector dimensions and similar sample scores lead engineers to propose mixing old and new vectors. Which migration supports consistent retrieval and rollback before switching all queries?

options.text: Mix both generations and normalize vector lengths, treating equal dimensions as a shared semantic coordinate system.
options.why: Normalization controls magnitude but does not align independently learned coordinate spaces, so comparable dimensions cannot justify cross-model similarity comparisons.

options.text: Switch query embeddings first, re-embedding older records only when users open them in the mixed index.
options.why: New queries against old vectors remain mismatched throughout migration, making retrieval inconsistent before the acceptance criteria have been established.

options.text: Build a separate new-model corpus index, evaluate matched queries and switch a versioned alias after acceptance.
options.why: Equal vector dimensions do not establish compatible embedding spaces; a complete parallel index supports matched evaluation and a clear rollback boundary.

options.text: Merge both models’ raw similarity scores and return the largest because their score ranges match.
options.why: A shared numerical range does not make scores calibrated or comparable across embedding models; raw maximum selection can distort result ordering.

questions.decision: Treat an embedding change as an index-version migration. Build and evaluate a complete matched corpus/query pair, switch an alias only after acceptance, and retain the prior pair for rollback. Equal dimensionality is a storage property, not proof that two models share a meaningful similarity space.

questions.title: Use exact sets for exact totals
questions.stem: A water authority needs exact unpaid commercial-meter charges for a district at the billing cutoff, including reversals and partial payments. Which retrieval design computes that total under existing account permissions and accounting rules?

options.text: Retrieve district tariffs and derive unpaid charges from policy documents and average commercial consumption.
options.why: Tariffs and average consumption cannot supply actual partial payments and reversals, which are necessary facts in the requested historical balance calculation.

options.text: Use an authorized query implementing district, cutoff, account-type and reversal rules; return total and parameters.
options.why: Exact totals require the complete qualifying set and defined accounting semantics; a constrained query can enforce both access and calculation rules.

options.text: Embed each account’s unpaid balance and retrieve as many descriptions as fit the context window.
options.why: Larger retrieval does not establish that every qualifying account and adjustment is included, and fitting text does not guarantee correct aggregation semantics.

options.text: Retrieve semantically similar bills and extrapolate the district total from that representative account sample.
options.why: Similarity retrieval is neither complete filtering nor a justified statistical sample, so extrapolation cannot establish the requested exact accounting total.

questions.decision: Match the operation to the data question: this is a filtered accounting aggregate over a complete authorized set. Use a query with explicit cutoff and adjustment semantics, then let language generation explain the returned result. Document similarity cannot establish an exact total over transactional records.

questions.title: Keep relationship authority explicit
questions.stem: A consortium needs all laboratories indirectly dependent on a specified calibration-standard revision and permitted exception rationales. A maintained graph has versioned edges; meeting notes explain exceptions. Select TWO retrieval components that fit.

options.text: Search similar instrument names and treat laboratories in top-ranked notes as the complete dependency closure.
options.why: Mention similarity does not prove reachability or completeness, and top-ranked prose may omit indirect dependents or include irrelevant laboratory references.

options.text: Retrieve permitted exception notes linked to resulting nodes and preserve source references in the explanation.
options.why: The notes add semantic rationale to an already computed set while retaining source evidence and the user’s access restrictions on exception content.

options.text: Infer dependency direction from document dates and rank laboratories by how recently their notes changed.
options.why: Edit timing does not encode the maintained relationship rules or identify all revision-specific paths in the authoritative dependency graph.

options.text: Traverse authorized, versioned edges from the specified revision under graph rules to compute downstream laboratories.
options.why: Relationship traversal provides explicit reachability over the maintained graph, including revision-specific edges that prose similarity cannot reliably enumerate completely.

options.text: Prompt with every edge and note, selecting the most consequential laboratories for a persuasive impact narrative.
options.why: The user requires complete defined reachability, not persuasive selection, and unrestricted note loading can exceed the user’s permitted exception scope.

questions.decision: Separate exact relationship computation from explanatory retrieval. Traverse the authorized graph for the specified revision, then fetch linked permitted notes to explain exceptions. This preserves completeness under the graph’s defined semantics while using language retrieval for the unstructured rationale it handles well.

questions.title: Reuse an existing controlled interface
questions.stem: One batch application calls a private tile-validation service through a tested client library. No other clients need discovery, and calls must stay inside the network boundary. Which integration fits instead of a hosted MCP façade and autonomous agent?

options.text: Place service credentials and client documentation in the prompt so Claude can construct network requests.
options.why: The application can execute a narrow authenticated operation without exposing credentials or granting the model broad responsibility for private network request construction.

options.text: Delegate validation to another autonomous agent because every tool call requires an agent to interpret results.
options.why: A deterministic validation service does not inherently require delegated reasoning, and another agent introduces orchestration without a stated capability need.

options.text: Host a public MCP façade because every model tool requires discovery despite fixed interfaces and callers.
options.why: MCP discovery is useful for reuse, but it is not a universal requirement for a single application calling a known private service.

options.text: Wrap the existing client in one narrow application tool, retaining private-network authentication and validation behavior.
options.why: The single known application path needs a controlled deterministic call, and the existing tested client already supplies the required service integration.

questions.decision: Choose the smallest integration that meets the known interface and trust boundary. A direct application tool around the tested client library preserves existing controls and avoids unnecessary hosting and delegation. MCP can be valuable for shared discovery, but this workload supplies no such reuse requirement.

questions.title: Separate delegation from raw tooling
questions.stem: A localization partner accepts bounded dialect reviews and returns evidence-backed decisions through its own expert workflow. It will not expose its terminology database. Select TWO contract terms beyond transport authentication and ownership of final publication.

options.text: Define delegated scope, allowed inputs, completion schema and how to report uncertainty or unresolved disputes.
options.why: An autonomous partner needs a task-level contract that distinguishes a completed review from a plausible but unsupported or unresolved answer.

options.text: Accept fluent explanations as complete and let the publication model infer any missing supporting evidence.
options.why: Fluency and inferred evidence do not satisfy a task acceptance contract, especially when proprietary internals are intentionally unavailable to the caller.

options.text: Require a raw MCP database export because delegation cannot yield usable decisions without internal-tool access.
options.why: Task delegation can respect the partner’s internal boundary; raw database disclosure is explicitly outside the agreed capability and is not inherently required.

options.text: Define timeouts, cancellation, correlation IDs and acceptance checks to handle late or invalid results deterministically.
options.why: Delegation crosses operational boundaries, so lifecycle controls and validation are necessary to keep a stalled or malformed result from blocking publication indefinitely.

options.text: Share publication credentials so completed partner reviews can directly update final material without additional checks.
options.why: The partner is delegated review, while final publication authority remains with the caller; credential sharing would expand authority beyond that contract.

questions.decision: Delegate a bounded review task, not hidden publication authority. The caller needs a semantic result contract plus operational controls for timeouts, cancellation and validation. Respecting the partner’s proprietary tools is compatible with requiring evidence and explicit uncertainty in the result used for publication decisions.

video_evidence.concept: Delegate to an independently reasoning partner

questions.title: Discovery must preserve semantic hints
questions.stem: An engineering assistant defers most of its 180 rare tools behind search. Slope-stability requests find hydrology tools because descriptions use internal nicknames. Which change improves discovery while retaining on-demand loading of detailed definitions?

options.text: Use shorter internal identifiers and infer meaning from identifiers frequent in previously successful sessions.
options.why: Opaque identifiers remove the capability information discovery needs, and historical frequency does not establish relevance to the current engineering request.

options.text: Describe user-facing capabilities and limits; test discovery recall and tool selection on representative queries.
options.why: Deferred tools must remain semantically discoverable; meaningful capability summaries and end-to-end tests address the mismatch between user language and internal nicknames.

options.text: Load every full definition permanently because a discovery failure establishes that deferral cannot select accurately.
options.why: The failure identifies poor retrieval descriptions, not a universal impossibility of progressive discovery, and full loading restores the original unnecessary context burden.

options.text: Randomly distribute tools among specialists and route requests to the least busy agent without catalog search.
options.why: Random partitions and load-based selection do not ensure the chosen agent has the relevant engineering capability or understands the user’s requested analysis.

questions.decision: Progressive discovery reduces loaded definitions only when its index can find the correct capability. Retain concise, user-facing semantic summaries and evaluate both discovery recall and final selection. Shortening away the distinguishing engineering purpose would undermine the mechanism that makes deferred loading useful.

questions.title: Choose the right economic denominator
questions.stem: Two annotation configurations pass scientific quality on the same workload. The table includes all attempts and inference expense, counting each accepted annotation once. Which has lower observed inference cost per accepted annotation, without double-counting failures?

options.text: B costs 0.027 units per accepted annotation, dividing recorded expense by all 1,000 attempts.
options.why: Attempts are the wrong denominator for this decision; the requested measure is expense per unique accepted annotation, not expense per attempted call.

options.text: A costs 0.067 units per accepted annotation, multiplying recorded expense by a repeat-until-success factor.
options.why: The data already include failed-attempt expense, so adding a hypothetical retry multiplier double-counts failures and imposes an unsupported stochastic model.

options.text: A costs 0.04 units per accepted annotation and B costs 0.03; B wins this comparison.
options.why: Divide recorded total expense by unique accepted outputs; failures are already included, giving 24/600 and 27/900 without another retry multiplier.

options.text: A wins because total expense is three units lower and all attempts undergo the same review.
options.why: Lower total expense does not establish lower cost per accepted annotation when accepted counts differ substantially between the two measured configurations.

questions.decision: Use observed expense divided by accepted outputs: A is 24/600 = 0.04 units; B is 27/900 = 0.03. B therefore wins this narrow inference-cost criterion. The table already includes failed attempts, so neither another retry factor nor an attempt denominator belongs in the calculation.

questions.title: Measure unsupported claims directly
questions.stem: A genealogy service scores answers by whether they contain a citation. Nearly all pass, yet some cite real census pages for incorrect household assignments. Which metric detects that failure while allowing accurate paraphrases?

options.text: Score exact overlap with a reference narrative, reducing credit for every differently worded historical paraphrase.
options.why: Exact wording overlap penalizes valid paraphrases and does not directly evaluate whether the cited census evidence supports the asserted household relationship.

options.text: Score reader satisfaction with fluency, relying on clear prose to reveal unsupported family relationships.
options.why: Fluency and satisfaction do not establish historical support, particularly when a plausible mistaken household assignment is difficult for users to notice.

options.text: Count unique census citations, requiring more pages when a narrative mentions several household names.
options.why: Citation quantity does not establish that the pages support the specific identity mapping, and extra citations can accompany the same unsupported claim.

options.text: Score evidence support for each material identity and relationship claim, allowing documented uncertainty and paraphrase.
options.why: Claim-level support checks the actual failure: a real citation may exist while the household identity or relationship asserted is unsupported.

questions.decision: Citation presence is a formatting signal. The required quality measure asks whether the evidence supports each consequential identity and relationship assertion. A rubric can accept paraphrase while rejecting an unsupported household assignment, and should distinguish uncertainty from a confident claim the source does not establish.

questions.title: Evaluate graders before trusting scores
questions.stem: Radio curators disagree on ambiguous speaker identities. An LLM judge’s agreement score mixes these disputes with clear cases; management proposes a tutorial’s universal threshold. Select TWO changes that make the judge’s fitness interpretable.

options.text: Report consequential false passes and failures by case type; retain human review where reliability is unproven.
options.why: Aggregate agreement can conceal the error direction that matters to release, so case-level risk and demonstrated scope should guide automation decisions.

options.text: Remove disputed cases permanently and stop recording uncertainty to stabilize the agreement denominator across releases.
options.why: Excluding ambiguity can support one clear-case measure, but removing it entirely prevents evaluation of uncertainty handling in the real archival task.

options.text: Separate clear and ambiguous cases, adjudicate uncertainty rules and evaluate independently labeled held-out examples.
options.why: Agreement has meaning only relative to a defined labeling task; separating ambiguity prevents unresolved human disagreements from obscuring clear-case judge behavior.

options.text: Adopt the tutorial threshold if pooled agreement passes, regardless of errors on unsupported factual assertions.
options.why: A generic threshold cannot resolve task-specific error consequences, and pooled agreement can hide systematic false passes on the archive’s critical cases.

options.text: Let the judge relabel curator disagreements and count agreement with those labels as independent human validation.
options.why: Labels generated by the judge are not independent evidence of that judge’s accuracy and would create circular validation on disputed cases.

questions.decision: Validate the judge against a clear, independently grounded rubric and examine error consequences, not just agreement. Separate ambiguity from clear mistakes and retain oversight where reliability is unproven. A tutorial’s threshold may motivate investigation, but it cannot certify fitness for every task and error distribution.
