questions.title: Keep regression evidence out of tuning
questions.stem: A satellite team repeatedly tuned prompts against 120 scenes, exposing expected findings during every revision. New labeled scenes span other seasons and sensors. Which dataset design supports release estimation while retaining development hard cases and regression tracking?

options.text: Rename the reused benchmark a release set and average its scores with model-reported scene confidence.
options.why: Renaming does not remove adaptation to the cases, and self-confidence does not provide an independent estimate of performance on unseen imagery.

options.text: Discard fixed hard cases and release using the easiest new scenes to make grading more consistent.
options.why: Dropping regressions and selecting easy holdout cases biases the release evidence away from the seasonal and sensor conditions the product must handle.

options.text: Use all labeled scenes in further tuning and interpret improved scores as evidence of seasonal generalization.
options.why: Once every scene informs tuning, none remains independent release evidence, so the result cannot establish generalization beyond the repeatedly exposed material.

options.text: Keep development regressions and reserve a separate release set stratified by season and sensor.
options.why: Separate roles preserve useful known failures while preventing repeatedly exposed development cases from being the sole estimate of performance on unseen data.

questions.decision: Retain known failures as regression assets, but do not confuse a tuned benchmark with independent release evidence. Use an unseen set stratified by relevant seasons and sensors for generalization estimates. Distinct dataset roles let the team learn from errors without overstating how well it handles new scenes.

questions.title: A bundle test estimates a bundle
questions.stem: A website randomizes visitors between an incumbent assistant and a bundle changing prompt, model and retrieval. The primary outcome improves and guardrails pass with adequate follow-up. Randomization and instrumentation are sound. Select TWO warranted conclusions.

options.text: Changing several components prevents the experiment from estimating any causal effect despite randomized assignment.
options.why: Randomization still identifies the effect of the assigned bundle; the limitation concerns component attribution rather than the existence of any interpretable comparison.

options.text: Deploy the prompt alone because the simpler component must preserve the successful bundle’s measured advantage.
options.why: The untested prompt-only configuration can behave differently, especially when components interact, so the bundle result does not establish its isolated performance.

options.text: Attributing gains to the prompt requires further controlled comparisons or a suitable component-level experiment.
options.why: The bundle comparison does not isolate component contributions, so the prompt may help, harm or interact with the other changes inside the winning package.

options.text: The agreed decision rule can support deployment because randomization estimates the tested bundle’s combined effect.
options.why: Multiple simultaneous component changes do not invalidate a randomized comparison of the package that was actually assigned and evaluated against the agreed gates.

options.text: Credit the prompt with the entire gain because it appeared first and controls interpretation of retrieval.
options.why: Implementation order in documentation does not isolate causal contribution, and plausible mechanism alone cannot attribute the observed effect to one component.

questions.decision: A sound randomized test can estimate a bundled intervention’s effect. If the preregistered outcome and guardrails pass, keeping that tested package may be justified. The same result cannot identify the prompt’s individual contribution; use component comparisons before claiming or deploying a prompt-only causal explanation.

video_evidence.concept: Separate package effects from component effects

questions.title: Respect paired evidence
questions.stem: Two prompts each run four times on the same 80 itineraries. Difficulty correlates within itineraries; the new prompt gains five percentage points. Engineers treat 320 runs as independent and apply a universal 1/√n margin. Which analysis fits?

options.text: Treat runs as independent itineraries because stochastic generation removes dependence on input difficulty and ambiguity.
options.why: Stochastic variation does not eliminate shared input effects, so repeated trials on one itinerary do not provide the same independent coverage as new itineraries.

options.text: Discard incumbent case outcomes and compare only the new prompt’s pooled pass rate with the desired gain.
options.why: Removing the paired baseline prevents estimation of the observed difference and confuses a target improvement with an absolute performance threshold.

options.text: Declare significance whenever the gain exceeds the tutorial margin, treating it as exact for paired binary comparisons.
options.why: A universal formula cannot capture all pairing, dependence and outcome-rate conditions, so applying it mechanically overstates the evidence in this design.

options.text: Analyze paired itinerary outcomes with repeated-run uncertainty; add independent itineraries if the result remains inconclusive.
options.why: Shared case difficulty violates the proposed independent-case assumption; paired case-aware analysis preserves the comparison and reflects the limited independent coverage.

questions.decision: The independent unit here is the itinerary, with repeated stochastic runs nested within it. Preserve pairing and account for that dependence when estimating uncertainty. More repeats help characterize variability on known cases, but broader independent itinerary coverage may be needed before declaring a small gain reliable.

questions.title: Distinguish truncation from bad data
questions.stem: An energy-audit app returns incomplete structured reports. Three traces share one prompt version. The owner wants to fix the dominant length defect while retaining mandatory business validation. Which diagnostic action does the table support for R1?

options.text: Disable schema checks because successful transport establishes partial JSON as a complete report for downstream consumers.
options.why: HTTP success does not establish report completeness, and accepting partial output would bypass the required structured and business-validation boundary.

options.text: Investigate output cap and report size, retaining schema and business checks when retrying or splitting R1.
options.why: The recorded max_tokens stop reason and incomplete object support output truncation; the repair should retain validation rather than erase the structured interface.

options.text: Refresh retrieval because an incomplete structured report necessarily indicates missing source passages in its context.
options.why: The specific stop reason identifies a different immediate mechanism, and missing evidence does not inherently explain an object cut off at the output cap.

options.text: Treat R1 as an authorization refusal and repeat with the same cap until the full object appears.
options.why: The trace records max_tokens rather than refusal, and repeating the same limiting configuration does not address a report whose output exceeds that cap.

questions.decision: Start with the actual stop reason. R1 hit its output cap, so investigate output size, a suitable cap or bounded report splitting while preserving validation. This evidence does not support a retrieval-first repair, treating truncation as refusal, or accepting an incomplete object as a successful business result.

questions.title: Isolate retrieval and generation faults
questions.stem: A horticulture assistant recommends a discontinued treatment despite current guidance in its trace. Superseded text appears first, and prompts say both “prefer first relevant” and “follow latest approved.” Select TWO steps addressing these known mechanisms.

options.text: Make first-ranked passages authoritative and keep latest-revision priority only as a tie-breaking preference.
options.why: This institutionalizes the contradictory priority and can continue selecting an obsolete first-ranked passage despite a newer approved revision being available.

options.text: Resolve conflicting priority rules and test generation against frozen context containing both revisions and authoritative metadata.
options.why: Frozen evidence isolates the instruction conflict and tests whether the generator follows the approved revision rule when both candidates are visibly available.

options.text: Delete the failing trace after editing so evaluation covers only guidance with one unambiguous revision.
options.why: Removing the reproducing case loses regression protection against the real multi-version condition that caused the discontinued recommendation to surface.

options.text: Use a stronger model for all requests and remove version metadata so prose quality determines currency.
options.why: Removing explicit metadata makes the temporal decision harder, and a model upgrade does not resolve contradictory instructions or establish correct retrieval behavior.

options.text: Test effective-version retrieval so later indexing or ranking changes cannot silently restore superseded-source priority.
options.why: Generation and retrieval are separate failure boundaries, and regression coverage should catch future reintroduction of obsolete evidence into a privileged position.

questions.decision: The trace identifies two actionable boundaries: contradictory generation instructions and retrieval that elevates superseded evidence. Freeze context to test the first repair, then add version-aware retrieval regression cases. Do not infer a model capability deficit before removing the known instruction and evidence-selection defects.

questions.title: Calculate cache savings by category
questions.stem: Using the fictional billing table, 100 calls each have 1,000 input and 100 output tokens. Every call has 800 cache-hit and 200 uncached input tokens. No writes, retries or other charges apply. What total and all-uncached savings follow?

options.text: Cost is 0.224 units: cached tokens still occupy context, so charge them at uncached input rates.
options.why: Context occupancy and billing category are distinct; the table explicitly assigns cached reads a different rate from ordinary uncached input.

options.text: Cost is 0.044 units: bill cache hits at the read rate and treat uncached tokens as free.
options.why: Uncached input is explicitly billable in the table; omitting its 0.040-unit contribution produces an unsupported discount for those tokens.

options.text: Cost is 0.080 units, saving 0.144 against the fictional all-uncached total of 0.224 units.
options.why: Cached input costs 0.016, uncached input 0.040 and output 0.024; their sum is 0.080 versus 0.224 without cache reads.

options.text: Cost is 0.056 units: output tokens are already part of each call’s 1,000 input tokens.
options.why: The scenario specifies output separately, so excluding its 0.024-unit charge understates the actual total under the fictional billing schedule.

questions.decision: Calculate each category separately using the hypothetical schedule. Cached reads: 80,000/1,000,000 × 0.20 = 0.016. Uncached input: 20,000 × 2/1,000,000 = 0.040. Output: 10,000 × 2.40/1,000,000 = 0.024. Total 0.080; all-uncached total 0.224, so savings are 0.144 units.

questions.title: Reconcile telemetry before blaming demand
questions.stem: A translation platform’s invoice rises after adding a reusable prefix, but completed jobs stay steady. Application spans count uncached input and output; billing exports also include cache creation and reads. Which monitoring repair supports accountable attribution?

options.text: Distribute unexplained expense equally across tenants because application traces always outrank billing exports as evidence.
options.why: Equal allocation is unsupported and incomplete traces cannot overrule billing-category evidence; telemetry coverage and attribution must be reconciled rather than assumed.

options.text: Remove the prefix because a post-change invoice discrepancy proves caching costs more than uncached inference.
options.why: The discrepancy may reflect omitted categories rather than poor economics, so removing the prefix before reconciliation confuses measurement completeness with configuration value.

options.text: Reconcile all billable categories with billing exports by tenant, feature and configuration, documenting telemetry gaps.
options.why: A complete category reconciliation tests the identified accounting omission while retaining the dimensions needed to attribute cost and explain residual measurement differences.

options.text: Double span-derived costs because the invoice increased after context changed while completed-job counts stayed stable.
options.why: An arbitrary factor cannot establish which categories are missing or which tenants caused expense, even if it temporarily makes aggregate totals appear similar.

questions.decision: Reconcile the accounting boundary before optimizing the system. Uncached input and output alone omit relevant categories when caching is active. Combine complete billable usage with tenant and configuration identifiers, then document any uninstrumented traffic so cost decisions rest on reconciled evidence instead of an arbitrary dashboard multiplier.

questions.title: Guard the actual side effect
questions.stem: Publication requires signed approval covering a supplier specification revision, product family and recipient list. Specifications and recipients can change afterward. All designs authenticate operators and retain audits. Select TWO additional controls that enforce the publication policy.

options.text: Validate current specification revision and recipient-set digest against approval inside the operation before external sending.
options.why: The approval must cover the actual publication state; tool-side comparison closes the gap created by changes between review and execution.

options.text: Invalidate approval or require renewal after material changes to product family, specification or recipients.
options.why: The owner’s approval scope includes each of these fields, so material mutations cannot inherit an authorization for an earlier, different publication state.

options.text: Allow publication when no confidential phrases are detected, retaining approval only for later accountability review.
options.why: Content screening addresses disclosure risk but cannot replace the owner’s explicit requirement for a signed approval bound to the publication’s state.

options.text: Display approval IDs in previews while accepting any approved revision of the specification during publication.
options.why: Displaying an identifier supports visibility but does not ensure the approval covers the revision and recipients that the operation actually publishes.

options.text: Check the specification hash at drafting and let operator identity cover later changes to recipients.
options.why: Draft-time integrity and operator authentication do not establish approval of the final recipient list after intervening edits to the publication request.

questions.decision: Authentication and auditability do not by themselves enforce approval scope. The side-effect operation must compare current publication state with the signed authorization, and material mutations require a fresh decision. Bind specification, product family and recipients so an apparently approved job cannot publish a different external disclosure.

video_evidence.concept: Enforce policy at the action boundary

questions.title: Treat evidence and authority separately
questions.stem: A berth-reservation agent reads a signed port bulletin containing useful schedules and instructions to reserve an unrelated expensive berth. Publishers lack purchasing authority; company policy requires explicit approval. Select THREE controls preserving evidence while limiting side effects.

options.text: Discard bulletins with imperative verbs and skip approval checks on those with only factual-looking content.
options.why: Imperative wording is not a complete instruction detector, and content appearance cannot replace the independent company approval required for consequential reservations.

options.text: Test realistic instruction-bearing bulletins for useful extraction and blocking of unauthorized reservation attempts.
options.why: Realistic adversarial cases assess the combined requirement: retaining legitimate evidence while resisting an instruction path that crosses the purchasing authority boundary.

options.text: Label fetched bulletins by source and treat their contents as untrusted data rather than agent instructions.
options.why: Publisher authenticity can support evidence provenance, but it does not grant the bulletin author authority over the broker’s instructions or purchasing workflow.

options.text: Require the reservation operation to validate separate approval covering berth, price and voyage before commitment.
options.why: A tool-side approval check limits consequential action even if the agent misinterprets a third-party instruction embedded in otherwise useful scheduling evidence.

options.text: Follow signed bulletin instructions and log reservations because authenticated publishers already supply operational information.
options.why: Authority to publish port information is not authority to reserve a berth for the broker, and logging does not supply the missing purchasing approval.

questions.decision: Keep provenance distinct from authority. A signed bulletin may provide useful facts while carrying instructions the broker never authorized. Treat it as untrusted data, enforce approval in the reservation operation and test the complete extraction-plus-action boundary with realistic adversarial content rather than relying on signatures or keywords.

questions.title: Surface the denominator and method
questions.stem: An analytics service calculates irrigation efficiency using hectares planted rather than hectares irrigated. Arithmetic is correct, but reviewers see only the plausible final ratio. Which change directly addresses this failure while retaining deterministic calculation?

options.text: Have Claude recalculate from the same planted-hectare inputs and display any disagreement with the service.
options.why: Repeating the calculation with the same wrong denominator can agree perfectly while leaving the actual irrigation-efficiency definition untested and incorrect.

options.text: Test division precision and display more decimal places to distinguish ratio changes between successive reports.
options.why: Precision tests are useful but do not verify which area measure belongs in the denominator; more decimals cannot repair the semantic input choice.

options.text: Have two reviewers independently approve the final ratio without exposing inputs or the metric definition.
options.why: Independent review of an opaque number does not reveal the denominator mismatch, so both reviewers can plausibly approve the same incorrectly defined metric.

options.text: Return numerator, denominator definition, period and calculation version; review against the agreed metric.
options.why: Correct arithmetic can implement the wrong metric; exposing semantic inputs and method lets reviewers verify that the denominator matches the business question.

questions.decision: The defect is semantic, not arithmetic. Make the formula’s inputs and definitions visible and validate them against the agreed metric. A deterministic service can calculate the wrong business ratio perfectly; reproducible method, source period and denominator identity let reviewers detect that mismatch before relying on the number.

questions.title: Review the diff that matters
questions.stem: Scientific editors approve textbook corrections but miss changed units and uncertainty ranges in polished replacement paragraphs. Editors must retain final publication authority. Which review design makes approval meaningful for this specific failure?

options.text: Assign paragraph confidence labels and send only low-confidence replacements through the existing full-paragraph approval screen.
options.why: Uncalibrated confidence does not identify the missed unit changes, and the proposal weakens review coverage without repairing the information shown to editors.

options.text: Show a semantic diff with quantities, units, sources and uncertainty; require flagged scientific changes to be resolved.
options.why: The review interface exposes the consequential differences and evidence editors currently cannot inspect efficiently, making their retained approval authority operationally meaningful.

options.text: Have a second editor read the same replacement paragraph after approval and record both reviewers’ names.
options.why: A second signature may add attention, but the same opaque presentation leaves both reviewers without the changed-value comparison and supporting source evidence.

options.text: Require a fixed minimum reading time and use logged duration as the primary proof of scientific review.
options.why: Time spent is a process proxy; it does not establish that the editor saw the unit change or checked the supporting scientific evidence.

questions.decision: Human approval must be supported by information that exposes the actual risk. A semantic diff, cited scientific evidence and explicit changed-value resolution help editors inspect the correction rather than merely read fluent replacement prose. Review duration or additional signatures cannot substitute for that task-specific evidence presentation.

questions.title: Calibrate a selective review policy
questions.stem: An archaeological catalog auto-accepts dates above an uncalibrated routing-score threshold. Auto-accepted error must stay below an agreed bound; rare imported collections lack labels. Select TWO changes that support selective automation with credible error assurance.

options.text: Measure only human-reviewed suggestions and use their error rate to certify suggestions bypassing review.
options.why: Reviewed and accepted populations are selected differently, so errors in one do not establish the conditional error rate required for the other.

options.text: Average catalogers’ personal thresholds to create a collection-neutral institutional confidence standard for automated acceptance.
options.why: Averaging subjective cutoffs does not calibrate accepted-output risk or establish sufficient labeled evidence for any particular collection under the agreed bound.

options.text: Estimate auto-accept error by collection on independent labels; set thresholds and review under-supported collections.
options.why: Selective automation needs evidence about errors in the accepted population, and sparse collections cannot inherit reliability established on unrelated well-labeled material.

options.text: Audit stratified auto-accepted samples and give an owner responsibility for evaluation updates and threshold review.
options.why: Ongoing sampling observes the population otherwise hidden from reviewers and can reveal collection shifts or failure patterns missed by the initial calibration data.

options.text: Raise every collection’s cutoff equally and interpret the new score directly as the probability of correctness.
options.why: A higher uncalibrated score does not acquire probabilistic meaning, and a uniform threshold ignores the sparse evidence for rare imported collections.

questions.decision: Calibrate against errors among the items the system intends to accept automatically. Validate by collection, reserve insufficiently evidenced groups for review and sample accepted outputs after launch. A threshold is a policy lever; its safety comes from measured conditional outcomes and continued oversight rather than the score’s appearance.

questions.title: Scope erasure as an executable obligation
questions.stem: A privacy owner confirms erasure covers identifiable attendee data in logs, retrieval chunks and evaluation examples, with no retention exception. Sources have attendee IDs; derived stores do not. Which design enables deletion and evidence of completion?

options.text: Obtain committee approval and count the approval email as completion before locating all derived records.
options.why: Approval records a decision but not execution; the architecture still lacks the traceability and deletion verification needed for the confirmed multi-store obligation.

options.text: Delete source records and exclude derived examples from model calls while retaining identifiable copies for analysts.
options.why: Exclusion from use does not fulfill the expressly confirmed deletion scope, which includes identifiable derived copies rather than the source row alone.

options.text: Map identities to derived records, delete across confirmed stores and retain minimal authorized completion evidence.
options.why: The stipulated decision requires locating derived copies, deleting them within scope and demonstrating completion without unnecessarily retaining the erased identifiable content itself.

options.text: Remove log names and treat derived copies as anonymous once their source attendee rows are deleted.
options.why: Removing one identifier or source link does not establish that remaining derived content is non-identifiable, and the owner has explicitly included those copies.

questions.decision: Implement the privacy owner’s scoped decision as a traceable data operation. Derived stores need identity linkage sufficient to find affected copies, deletion jobs need verifiable outcomes, and any retained completion record must be minimized and authorized. This scenario stipulates applicability and no exception rather than asserting a universal erasure rule.

questions.title: Review the deployed processing route
questions.stem: A transport workload must stay inside an authorized cloud boundary. Provider certification names a service and region, but the assistant exports traces to an unapproved commercial analytics account. What resolves this application-level gap before sensitive deployment?

options.text: Retain analytics exports without payload text, treating all metadata transfers as inside the certified boundary.
options.why: Payload minimization can reduce exposure, but metadata classification and destination approval still matter; it does not automatically place a separate account inside the boundary.

options.text: Map model, storage and telemetry routes; remove or approve analytics transfers and document customer controls.
options.why: Provider evidence can support its named boundary, but the application’s additional telemetry destination and customer responsibilities must be reviewed in the actual deployment context.

options.text: Accept certification as covering every downstream service whenever transfers use encryption and authenticated accounts.
options.why: Encryption and authentication do not extend the provider’s named authorization boundary to an independently operated analytics account outside the approved deployment route.

options.text: Wait for provider certification of the entire custom application, assigning all customer controls to the provider.
options.why: The agency still owns application-specific decisions and controls; provider evidence can be reused without requiring the provider to assume every custom integration obligation.

questions.decision: Certification evidence applies to a defined service boundary. Trace the deployed application’s model, storage and telemetry paths against that boundary, then resolve the unapproved transfer and customer controls with the owner. Reusing provider evidence is useful, but it cannot silently authorize an additional external processing route.

video_evidence.concept: Authorization applies to a service boundary

questions.title: Evaluate contestability and error direction
questions.stem: A scholarship foundation already uses human panels to review AI summaries. Policy additionally requires applicant notice, factual correction and monitoring for unequal harmful errors across relevant groups. Select TWO additions that close these stated obligations.

options.text: Explain the assistant’s role and provide an accessible correction route reaching the panel before final decisions.
options.why: Transparency and timely correction make the foundation’s stated policy operational; a later complaint channel cannot repair an already closed factual review window.

options.text: Report pooled human–AI agreement and treat a high overall rate as satisfying group-level monitoring obligations.
options.why: Pooled agreement can conceal unequal harmful errors, so it does not establish the specifically required comparison across relevant applicant groups.

options.text: Assess consequential omissions and adverse errors by group with sufficient evidence; escalate unexplained differences to the owner.
options.why: Harmful error direction and group-level outcomes test the stated concern more directly than pooled agreement, while ownership ensures differences lead to review.

options.text: Publish technical benchmark scores and allow applicants to contest outcomes only after selection has concluded.
options.why: A technical benchmark does not explain the assistant’s actual role, and a post-cycle challenge cannot meet the stated timely factual-correction obligation.

options.text: Remove applicant names and waive notice because a human panel retains every final selection decision.
options.why: Name removal does not eliminate proxy information, and retained human authority does not waive the foundation’s explicitly stipulated applicant-notice requirement.

questions.decision: The remaining requirements concern the assisted process around the panel: applicants need useful notice and a timely correction route, while owners need evidence about harmful errors across relevant groups. Human final review is already present; it does not by itself satisfy those independent transparency and fairness obligations.

questions.title: Give accountability an operating path
questions.stem: A heritage portal publishes an offensive description of a living community. Feedback enters an unassigned general inbox despite an incident policy. The content owner can withdraw and correct descriptions. Which change creates an accountable response process?

options.text: Move feedback to the homepage and rely on greater visibility to bring an eventual owner response.
options.why: Visibility improves reporting but does not establish triage, ownership, response targets or the authority needed to act on the reported public error.

options.text: Refer the incident to the model vendor and suspend internal investigation pending its usage-policy determination.
options.why: Vendor review may help, but it does not replace the portal’s authority and responsibility to contain and correct its currently published description.

options.text: Add the description to the next prompt benchmark and count test-set inclusion as incident resolution.
options.why: Regression evidence is useful for prevention but does not withdraw the current description, communicate with affected people or assign responsibility for correction.

options.text: Assign a content owner with response targets, withdrawal powers, community feedback and documented correction and retesting.
options.why: Named responsibility and executable authority connect reports to containment, correction and learning rather than leaving existing forms and policies without an accountable response.

questions.decision: Accountability requires a route from a report to an authorized person who can act. Assign ownership, containment and correction steps, response targets and follow-through into validation. Existing forms and policy text are useful only when they lead to a timely decision about the actual published content and its recurrence.

questions.title: Discover the decision window
questions.stem: An electricity-market sponsor measures report accuracy, but traders need evidence cards within a two-minute pre-auction window. Some interpretations require specialist signoff. Which discovery deliverable converts these findings into requirements before selecting models or research patterns?

options.text: Set a two-minute latency target and consider every timely interpretation within the assistant’s authorized scope.
options.why: The time requirement matters, but timeliness does not establish permission to make interpretations that compliance reserves for specialist signoff under the stated constraints.

options.text: Benchmark long-form reports first and choose briefing length after selecting the sponsor’s preferred strongest model.
options.why: The sponsor’s metric alone omits the observed time window and specialist authority, so a strong report benchmark can still validate an unusable workflow.

options.text: Draw retrieval, streaming and reviewer components, then ask traders to infer acceptance criteria from the diagram.
options.why: Components may eventually satisfy the need, but architecture-first inference leaves the workflow and authority requirements undefined when the solution is selected.

options.text: Agree the decision window, briefing scope, signoff boundary and measurable evidence-card acceptance criteria with owners.
options.why: The deliverable links observed workflow, decision authority and success criteria, supplying constraints that can actually distinguish feasible architectures before implementation choices begin.

questions.decision: Discovery must specify the decision the service supports, the time available and the authority it holds. Capture the observed evidence-card workflow and specialist boundary as owned acceptance criteria. Those requirements let later model and pattern comparisons demonstrate usability rather than merely produce accurate long-form reports.

video_evidence.concept: Observe users in their actual workflow

questions.title: Distinguish readiness from enthusiasm
questions.stem: An art-insurance sponsor approves funding and requests autonomous restoration advice next week. The readiness table leaves image rights, expert authority and acceptance criteria unresolved. Select TWO deliverables that support an evidence-backed go decision.

options.text: Issue conditional readiness with missing permissions and authority boundaries, assigning owners and required closure evidence.
options.why: A conditional decision identifies resolvable blockers and accountability instead of interpreting sponsor enthusiasm or budget approval as missing rights and delegated expertise.

options.text: Pilot the smallest model and treat lower inference costs as resolving all three discovery conditions.
options.why: Pilot labeling and lower token cost do not resolve image permission, decision authority or the absence of an expert-approved definition of a correct result.

options.text: Agree a measurable first task and acceptance dataset with conservators before selecting its bounded system function.
options.why: The team needs a testable permitted task and expert criteria before architecture choices can be judged against actual readiness rather than an undefined restoration promise.

options.text: Use synthetic conservation judgments as labels and let model recommendations define the expert acceptance standard.
options.why: Generated judgments cannot substitute for the unresolved expert decision standard, so this creates circular success criteria rather than evidence of domain readiness.

options.text: Start autonomous recommendations under approved funding and defer image permission until a compelling demonstration exists.
options.why: Budget approval does not grant missing image rights, and the proposed start accepts a capability whose expert authority remains explicitly unresolved in discovery.

questions.decision: A funded proposal can remain unready. State a conditional decision with owners and closure evidence, then define a bounded task and expert-approved acceptance cases. Rights, authority and success criteria shape the architecture; they are not implementation details that a cheaper model or pilot label can settle.

questions.title: Communicate the accepted trade-off
questions.stem: A documentary studio chooses a slower evidence-grounded transcript assistant because attribution accuracy is a release gate. Matched-task results support it, but ambiguous voices still need editors. How should engineers explain this choice to an executive?

options.text: Present full prompt and retrieval settings so the executive can infer why technical sophistication warrants slower completion.
options.why: Implementation detail can support engineering review but does not directly explain the release gate, economic consequence or remaining human work behind this decision.

options.text: Present public benchmark rank and claim grounding ensures ambiguous voices will never require editorial intervention.
options.why: Public rankings do not establish the studio’s matched task performance, and the stated residual ambiguity directly contradicts the promise of no remaining intervention.

options.text: Present only the faster tool’s attribution errors, omitting the selected design’s deadline costs to simplify approval.
options.why: A credible trade-off presentation includes material disadvantages and residual risk; omitting the deadline impact prevents an informed assessment of the actual recommendation.

options.text: Present the attribution gate, measured quality, delivered cost, deadline impact and remaining human-attribution cases with ownership.
options.why: This connects the recommendation to the business constraint and measured trade-off while making residual work and accountability visible to the decision-maker.

questions.decision: Explain the decision through the studio’s release obligation and measured task outcomes. Include the cost and deadline price of better attribution, plus the ambiguity still assigned to human editors. That makes the recommendation assessable without implying that technical grounding alone has removed every remaining editorial risk.

video_evidence.concept: Tailor decision evidence to its audience

questions.title: Record why a decision is revisitable
questions.stem: A municipal archive chooses full context for a small, stable catalog. Growth and record-level permissions may change that choice in six months. Select TWO ADR contents that let future teams reassess the decision.

options.text: Save a successful catalog answer as the design record, sufficient to reconstruct rejected implementation alternatives later.
options.why: One output does not establish alternatives, constraints or consequences, so future teams cannot infer the rationale or its validity under changed conditions.

options.text: Record alternatives, consequences and revisit triggers, including changed access scope or failed latency and quality gates.
options.why: Alternatives and triggers let future maintainers re-evaluate the decision when its premises change rather than treating the original choice as permanently normative.

options.text: Record only model ID and maximum tokens because these fully determine whether retrieval becomes necessary.
options.why: Model capacity alone does not capture permissions, freshness, retrieval overhead or observed task quality, all of which can change the architecture’s suitability.

options.text: Record corpus size, update rate, shared access scope and measured task behavior supporting this deployment’s choice.
options.why: The decision’s context explains its present fit, including constraints beyond size that may change when per-record permissions or update patterns are introduced.

options.text: Require full context below the article’s token guideline and model replacement before considering permission-aware retrieval.
options.why: A historical sizing heuristic is not a universal requirement and cannot override future authorization or freshness constraints specific to the archive’s deployment.

questions.decision: Record a conditional architectural judgment rather than a slogan. Full context can fit this catalog under its present permissions, stability and measured behavior. An ADR should preserve those premises, the alternatives and revisit triggers so a growing or newly permissioned catalog can be reassessed on evidence.

questions.title: Budget an explicit service promise
questions.stem: Availability means eligible rental-extension requests receiving valid confirmation within ten seconds; unauthorized requests are excluded. In a fixed 30-day window, 36 of 20,000 eligible requests fail. The target is 99.8%. Which result and remaining error budget are correct?

options.text: Availability is 99.82%; 36 of 40 allowed failures leave four before exceeding the fixed-window target.
options.why: There are 19,964 good requests out of 20,000, and 0.2% of the agreed denominator permits 40 failures, leaving four after 36.

options.text: Availability is 99.64%; subtract failures and successful retries because repeated attempts cannot count as confirmations.
options.why: The stipulated indicator counts eligible requests meeting the confirmation criterion; no additional failed-retry count is supplied or justified by the definition.

options.text: Availability is 99.82%; 36 failures consume 36% of the budget, one percentage point per failure.
options.why: Availability is correct, but budget consumption is 36/40 = 90%, not 36%; the target determines the allowed count in this denominator.

options.text: Availability is exactly 99.8%; round to target and report no budget consumed while the service passes.
options.why: Passing does not mean no budget has been spent, and rounding away the observed failures obscures that only four allowed failures remain in this window.

questions.decision: Use the agreed request denominator and good-event definition. Availability is (20,000 − 36)/20,000 = 99.82%. A 99.8% target allows 0.2% × 20,000 = 40 failures, so 36 consume 90% of the budget and four remain in this fixed window. Communicate that narrow margin.

questions.title: Make feedback a governed change stream
questions.stem: A language-access assistant explains appointment logistics. Users request court-order interpretation and report a reproducible appointment mistranslation. Legal scope is unchanged. Select THREE actions that improve the approved service while addressing demand for the new capability.

options.text: Route interpretation demand to policy-led discovery of scope, risks, data and acceptance requirements before delivery commitments.
options.why: User demand establishes a potential need, but the requested capability exceeds current authority and requires its own requirements and risk decision before implementation.

options.text: Add the appointment mistranslation as a regression case and validate its repair against existing workflow gates.
options.why: This failure belongs to the approved capability, so a tested repair can improve the current service without waiting for authority over a different task.

options.text: Add experimental court-order examples to the logistics prompt and retain existing gates because users requested both tasks.
options.why: Experimental wording does not supply the missing authority or evaluation coverage, and shared users do not make court interpretation equivalent to appointment logistics.

options.text: Use the established feedback channel to communicate repair progress and the process for deciding interpretation scope.
options.why: Users need visible disposition of both kinds of feedback, while clear status prevents an investigation of new demand being mistaken for an expanded service promise.

options.text: Delay the appointment repair until court-order policy is settled, then release one coherent language-support capability.
options.why: The known supported-flow defect has an independent repair path; bundling it with unresolved new authority unnecessarily prolongs an existing reproducible user harm.

questions.decision: Separate feedback by what it changes. Repair the reproducible in-scope defect through regression testing now, while the new interpretation demand returns to discovery with its own owner and acceptance criteria. Communicate both dispositions so users see action without being promised a capability whose authority is unresolved.

questions.title: Document the operational contract
questions.stem: Two polar field stations implement the same service overview but choose different timeout, retry and stale-data behavior. Intermittent networks then produce contradictory advice. Which documentation addition makes intended behavior implementable and testable at both stations?

options.text: Version contracts and runnable examples for timeout, retry, freshness and degraded replies; test both stations.
options.why: A behavioral contract supplies the missing obligations and test cases, making consistent implementation possible despite differing local networks and independently written clients.

options.text: Create an incident channel and have station engineers manually coordinate whenever outages produce different advice.
options.why: Communication helps during incidents but does not establish a reproducible implementation contract or prevent divergent stale-data behavior before operators encounter it.

options.text: Expand component names in the overview while leaving outage behavior local because both stations use the same services.
options.why: Additional structural detail does not define timeout, retry or freshness semantics, and local discretion preserves the contradictory operational behavior the program needs to resolve.

options.text: Record local timeouts in separate ADRs and accept any response that uses the overview’s shared service names.
options.why: Local decision records explain divergence but do not define shared conformance; identical component names do not imply consistent operational semantics under network failure.

questions.decision: An overview explains structure; implementers also need the behavior at each interface. Specify retry, timeout, freshness and degraded-response semantics with executable examples and conformance cases. That makes the cross-station contract reviewable and testable rather than leaving critical outage behavior to local inference from a diagram.

questions.title: Migrate a release unit
questions.stem: An aviation assistant’s model is retiring. Its prompt and parser are coupled; the replacement canary uses a new output contract. Rollback restores only the binary, leaving new configuration active. Which lifecycle change makes migration and rollback credible?

options.text: Version model, prompt, schema, parser and routing as a tested unit; validate replacement and rehearse supported rollback.
options.why: A coherent release unit prevents mixed-version rollback, and the fallback must remain available after retirement rather than relying on an unusable old model route.

options.text: Pin the retiring model permanently and delay parser migration because snapshots guarantee indefinite provider availability.
options.why: Pinning identifies a version but does not cancel retirement, so it cannot provide the supported long-term recovery path required by the lifecycle event.

options.text: Switch all traffic immediately but retain the old prompt to minimize changed files in the migration release.
options.why: Minimizing file changes does not establish semantic compatibility, and this bypasses the known need to test the prompt and parser with the replacement configuration.

options.text: Keep binary-only rollback and evaluate mixed prompt and parser versions during the first incident after retirement.
options.why: External configuration can still define behavior, and an untested mixed-version rollback is not a credible recovery path for the imminent model migration.

questions.decision: Migrate and recover a coherent behavior configuration, not just a binary. Test the replacement model with its prompt, schema, parser and routing, and rehearse a supported fallback. Because retirement can remove the old route, rollback planning must account for availability as well as version compatibility.

questions.title: Define handoff through demonstrated operation
questions.stem: An Antarctic logistics service deploys successfully with a runbook and named owner. Receiving operators have never handled stale weather or restored an evidence index. Select TWO handoff checks demonstrating they can operate and safely change it.

options.text: Use a general-knowledge model benchmark to prove future incidents need no service-configuration changes for resolution.
options.why: General model performance does not establish the receiving team’s ability to restore indexes, validate releases or operate the service’s concrete incident and change paths.

options.text: Accept the owner and runbook as sufficient because rehearsals duplicate the completed successful application deployment.
options.why: Deployment success does not establish that the receiving team can diagnose stale data, access recovery artifacts or execute the documented restoration procedure.

options.text: Have receiving operators rehearse stale-evidence incidents and restore compatible configuration under realistic access constraints.
options.why: Rehearsal demonstrates that documentation, permissions and recovery artifacts work together for the team that will actually operate the service after handoff.

options.text: Have builders run all rehearsals while operators watch dashboards, certifying readiness from the builders’ successful responses.
options.why: Builder competence does not demonstrate receiving-team access or operational ability, which is the specific unresolved handoff condition described in this scenario.

options.text: Transfer evaluations, configuration registry and change procedures; verify operators can test and deploy a controlled update.
options.why: Operations must support safe iteration as well as incident response; demonstrating the change path tests whether critical lifecycle assets and responsibilities truly transferred.

questions.decision: Handoff is demonstrated transfer of operation and safe change. The receiving team should rehearse realistic incidents with its actual permissions, then validate a controlled update using the transferred evaluation and configuration assets. A deployed service, a document and a named owner are necessary inputs, not proof of practical readiness.

questions.title: Separate contextual guidance from control
questions.stem: A coding assistant needs changing project conventions and an organization-wide restriction on a credential directory. The restriction must survive local preference changes. Which configuration assigns these requirements to appropriate mechanisms?

options.text: Put credential restrictions in editable personal settings and project conventions in central policy near organizational controls.
options.why: The non-overridable organizational requirement should not depend on editable personal preferences, while project conventions need not become uniform organization-wide policy.

options.text: Keep credential restrictions in a release-only skill because other coding tasks need not discover the restricted path.
options.why: A restriction must apply whenever access might occur, not only when a skill happens to load, and contextual loading is not an enforcement boundary.

options.text: Version project conventions in repository instructions; enforce credential access with managed permissions and verified OS controls.
options.why: Contextual conventions and enforceable access restrictions serve different roles; central policy and underlying controls can protect the directory despite local preference changes.

options.text: Put both requirements in root instructions and require signatures, treating acknowledgment as overriding tool permission settings.
options.why: Acknowledged instructions guide behavior but do not replace filesystem enforcement or establish precedence over the assistant’s actual configured access permissions.

questions.decision: Use context for conventions and enforcement for access. Version repository guidance so the team can review changes, while organizational restrictions live in centrally managed policy backed by verified filesystem controls. A natural-language instruction can explain a restriction but cannot by itself prevent the underlying file access.

questions.title: Hooks need failure semantics
questions.stem: A post-edit formatting hook fails on temporarily incomplete generated source. The assistant continues and CI rejects changes. The team wants quick local feedback and formatting assurance. Which design gives the hook a reliable acceptance boundary?

options.text: Block edits until future files are formatted, using the post-edit hook to predict whether new source parses.
options.why: A post-edit hook cannot establish a pre-edit property of future content, and this proposal does not define workable handling of intermediate source states.

options.text: Replace the hook with detailed project instructions, using guidance to ensure formatting even for temporarily incomplete files.
options.why: Contextual instructions do not guarantee execution or successful formatting, and they do not supply the missing enforced acceptance boundary after hook failures.

options.text: Count every hook invocation as formatting proof and suppress exit status because intermediate files may be invalid.
options.why: Invocation is not successful completion, and suppressing failures hides exactly the condition that lets unformatted code proceed to the later CI rejection.

options.text: Test the scoped hook and surface any failures; require a formatting check before protected-branch integration.
options.why: A hook can automate feedback but may fail; a required acceptance check enforces the repository outcome even when local formatting cannot complete successfully.

questions.decision: Hooks automate an action, but their success and failure behavior still needs design and testing. Surface local failures, scope the hook appropriately and retain an enforced formatting gate at integration. This distinguishes useful immediate feedback from the separate guarantee that accepted repository changes satisfy formatting requirements.

questions.title: Make generated review results actionable
questions.stem: An astronomy team’s CI assistant produces variable prose findings that become hard to place after new commits. Posting is separately authorized. Select TWO changes making findings reviewable without assuming structured syntax proves technical correctness.

options.text: Review file names alone and infer current line numbers from earlier findings to keep comments stable.
options.why: Stable-looking coordinates are not evidence of current locations, and reviewing names without the relevant diff cannot substantiate the proposed code-level technical finding.

options.text: Emit validated findings with relative paths, verified diff lines, severity, explanation and analyzed commit ID.
options.why: A stable contract removes prose parsing ambiguity and identifies the precise code state and location to which each technical assertion applies.

options.text: Publish every schema-valid record immediately, treating syntactic validation as proof of a bug at current head.
options.why: A schema validates shape, not technical truth or commit freshness, so syntactically valid records may still be wrong or refer to an obsolete diff.

options.text: Parse prose with updated regular expressions and omit commit IDs because a PR number uniquely identifies code state.
options.why: Pull requests have multiple heads over time, so the number cannot establish code freshness, and wording-dependent parsing preserves the original unstable interface.

options.text: Check findings against current diffs and required checks; suppress or refresh results if head changes before publication.
options.why: Structural validity does not establish current relevance or correctness; state checks and evidence review prevent old findings being attached to changed code.

questions.decision: CI review needs a stable data contract and a state-aware publication path. Structured records make findings parseable, but commit and diff verification establish relevance and evidence checks establish technical usefulness. If the head changes, refresh or suppress stale results rather than attaching plausible coordinates to a different code state.

questions.title: Build an evidence-preserving incident draft
questions.stem: A telescope outage record mixes time zones across alerts, deployments and operator messages. An assistant blames the first deployment mentioned in chat, but engineers have not reproduced the fault. Which method produces a reviewable postmortem while preserving uncertainty?

options.text: Adopt the first chat-mentioned deployment as cause and have Claude align the timeline before engineer review.
options.why: Narrative consistency cannot establish causation, and fitting events to the first chat hypothesis risks suppressing evidence that contradicts an initially plausible explanation.

options.text: Merge polished source summaries by paragraph length and count repeated claims as independent confirmation of cause.
options.why: Repeated claims can share one original assumption, while paragraph length does not resolve time zones or distinguish independent observations from copied speculation.

options.text: Link normalized timestamps, separate observations from hypotheses and have engineers verify chronology and test causes before publication.
options.why: An evidence-preserving draft accelerates synthesis while retaining temporal provenance and keeping unverified causation separate from facts until the accountable engineers review it.

options.text: Publish a preliminary factual postmortem because linked alerts independently verify every causal claim generated from them.
options.why: Source links establish traceability, not automatic causal verification, and publishing speculative conclusions as facts exceeds what the evidence currently supports.

questions.decision: Use the assistant to assemble and normalize evidence, not to promote the first plausible cause into fact. A source-linked timeline with explicit hypotheses gives engineers a useful draft. They must verify timing and test the causal account before owning and publishing the final incident conclusions.

drills.title: Evidence boundaries: judge each proposal
drills.stem: Judge each proposal independently against the stated obligation. Answer Yes or No for every row; no fixed number of Yes answers is implied.

rows.text: Requirement: approval covers the published illustration revision. Proposal: the send operation compares its current revision hash with the signed approval and rejects a mismatch.
rows.why: The check binds authorization to the actual state at the side effect.

rows.text: Requirement: all three independent checks pass before release. Proposal: parallel checks return results tagged with one frozen revision and an all-required join gates release.
rows.why: Concurrency preserves the mandatory completion condition when every result covers the same revision.

rows.text: Requirement: exact count of qualifying records. Proposal: vector search returns the most similar twenty records, whose count is presented as the full qualifying total.
rows.why: A similarity result is not proof of complete predicate-based enumeration.

rows.text: Requirement: identify the prompt’s individual causal contribution. Proposal: randomize users between two packages that differ in prompt, model and retrieval, then attribute the entire gain to the prompt.
rows.why: The comparison identifies the package effect rather than the prompt component alone.

rows.text: Requirement: preserve current access after queued work. Proposal: worker and delivery checks use current requester permissions rather than a submission-time permission snapshot alone.
rows.why: Revalidation addresses permission changes before the consequential read and delivery boundaries.

drills.title: Measurement claims: judge independently
drills.stem: Decide whether each conclusion follows from the explicitly stated evidence. Judge rows independently; these are supplemental unscored exercises.

rows.text: A service has 5,000 eligible requests and 15 failures. Against a 99.8% target it passes because fewer than twenty requests failed.
rows.why: The allowance is 0.2% of 5,000, or ten failures; fifteen exceeds it.

rows.text: A schema-valid output contains the wrong equipment revision. Schema validation alone has not established the business fact’s correctness.
rows.why: Valid structure and semantic correctness are separate acceptance obligations.

rows.text: Two embedding models have the same dimension. This establishes that their independently produced vectors can safely share one similarity index.
rows.why: Dimensional equality does not establish a shared learned coordinate space.

rows.text: All billable cache categories and ordinary input/output are reconciled to the billing export, with uninstrumented traffic recorded. The cost dashboard has a defensible reconciliation basis.
rows.why: The proposal covers category completeness and explicitly accounts for coverage differences.

rows.text: An asynchronous batch often finishes within an hour. This alone guarantees every future six-hour deadline will be met without fallback.
rows.why: Typical completion is not a guarantee, and unfinished or expired requests need explicit treatment.

drills.title: Choose the accountable artifact
drills.stem: Match each need to the artifact with the BEST primary purpose in this project. Choices may repeat; judge every row independently.

rows.text: Explain why the small stable catalog used full context and what permission change should trigger reconsideration.
rows.why: It retains the decision premises, alternatives and revisit conditions.

rows.text: Specify timeout, stale-data and retry behavior that two field-station clients must implement identically.
rows.why: These are observable obligations at the shared service boundary.

rows.text: Show the receiving operator how to detect an outdated index and restore a compatible known configuration.
rows.why: The primary need is an executable incident and recovery procedure.

rows.text: Retain held-out case definitions, grading versions and candidate results supporting release acceptance.
rows.why: This records the test evidence and reproducibility needed to assess acceptance.

rows.text: Explain why final scientific attribution remains with an editor despite a measured improvement from automatic drafts.
rows.why: It captures the authority choice and its supporting trade-off rationale.
